approachQuestion.prompt: A laboratory dispenses units in distinct positive batch sizes. Any size may be used repeatedly. Return the number of multisets of batches totaling exactly T, modulo 1000000007; order of dispensing does not distinguish answers. Examples: sizes=[1,2], T=3 → 2 ({1,1,1},{1,2}); sizes=[2,4], T=5 → 0. Which approach is most suitable?
constraints: 1 ≤ k=sizes.length ≤ 30; distinct sizes from 1 through 1000; 1 ≤ T ≤ 10000. Input is read-only. Return only a modular count.

options.text: Initialize ways[0]=1 and other sums to zero. Process sizes in their input order as the outer loop; for each size v update sums s=v..T upward by adding ways[s−v] modulo the modulus. Return ways[T].
options.feedback: Each outer iteration adds all multiplicities of one new batch size. A multiset is formed in exactly one size-processing order, while upward sums allow the current size to repeat.

options.text: Store ways for every prefix of sizes and every sum, using the previous row for omission and the current row at s−v for another batch.
options.feedback: This computes the correct result on the whole domain, but retains old states that future transitions never read. Removing those states preserves correctness and reduces auxiliary storage.

options.text: Loop sums on the outside and all sizes on the inside, adding ways[s−v].
options.feedback: For sizes=[1,2], T=3, this distinguishes [1,2] from [2,1] and returns 3 rather than 2.

options.text: Loop sizes outside but update sums downward.
options.feedback: For sizes=[2], T=4, this disallows repeating the size and returns zero; the multiset {2,2} is legal.

feedback.reason: Use size-first ascending updates to count unbounded combinations without counting order permutations.
details: Allocate T+1 modular counters and initialize only ways[0] to one. For each of k sizes visit all sums from that size upward to T. Return ways[T], retaining no prefix rows.

Process batch sizes outside the increasing-sum loop so permutations of the same multiset are not counted separately. Distinct positive sizes also bound how many sizes can update any target; k sizes above T still cost inspection.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Allocate T+1 modular counters and initialize only ways[0] to one. For each of k sizes visit all sums from that size upward to T. Return ways[T], retaining no prefix rows. Analyze this fixed implementation. N=k; k,T vary independently. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Array indexing and word arithmetic take constant time. No hashing, amortized containers, recursion, slicing, or input copying is used. Count all allocated work arrays and temporaries; exclude the read-only input and scalar output.
Include initialization; treat the stated dimensions as variable parameters within their bounds. Use a word per stored counter or flag, not a packed bitset.

options.text: O(k + T min(k,T)) time, O(T) auxiliary space
O(k + T min(k,T)) time, O(kT) auxiliary space
O(k + T min(k,T)) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Include k size checks and updates only for sizes at most T.
details: Initialization takes T+1 work and the outer loop inspects k sizes, even when they exceed T. Since sizes are distinct positive integers, at most min(k,T) sizes run an update loop. The maximum number of updates comes from the smallest sizes 1 through min(k,T): the sum of T−v+1 over these sizes is tightly proportional to T min(k,T). Thus total worst-case work is O(k + T min(k,T)). The single array contains T+1 counters; there are no multiset lists, hashes, copies, or recursive calls.

“O(kT) time, O(T) auxiliary space”: When k≤T this agrees with the tight bound. For independent k>T, only T distinct positive sizes can be eligible. The k outer checks plus at most a triangular number of sum updates give k + T² work, so kT can overestimate the tight worst case.
“O(k + T min(k,T)) time, O(kT) auxiliary space”: The time matches, but the fixed method stores only one array of T+1 counts, not a row for every size.
“O(k + T min(k,T)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The time matches, but in-place updates retain T+1 counters. This storage grows with T.
